summary: The SR&ED reporting deadline is the statutory cut-off for Canadian taxpayers to file Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 under subsection 37(11) of the Income Tax Act. Executive Overview and Macro-Fiscal Architecture of the Canadian SR&ED Regime

The Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Programme serves as the cornerstone of federal innovation policy in Canada, delivering non-dilutive capital to enterprises engaged in systematic scientific and technological advancement1. Administered jointly by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) and the Department of Finance Canada, the statutory framework is codified primarily within Section 37, Section 127, Section 127.1, and Subsection 248(1) of the federal Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)) alongside Part XXIX (Section 2900) of the Income Tax Regulations (C.R.C., c. 945)3. Originating in its modern structural form in 1985, the dual-incentive regime was engineered to overcome chronic private-sector underinvestment in research and development by pairing immediate tax deductibility with refundable and non-refundable investment tax credits6. For the fiscal year ended March 31, 2025, the SR&ED programme delivered $4.5 billion in investment tax credits (ITCs) across more than 22,000 processed claims supporting over 19,000 claimants2. By the fiscal year ended March 31, 2026, total SR&ED tax credits claimed reached $4.9 billion, with $4.6 billion formally allowed by the CRA—representing an expansion of approximately 50% in annual credit value since fiscal year 2022 and supporting more than 24,160 innovating businesses nationwide1.

Between late 2024 and early 2026, the federal SR&ED architecture underwent its most consequential legislative modernisation in over a decade2. Following public consultations initiated by the Department of Finance in early 2024 regarding both a patent box regime and SR&ED modernisation, alongside policy proposals tabled in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement on December 16, 2024, Parliament enacted Bill C-15, the Budget Implementation Act, 2025, No. 1, which received Royal Assent on March 26, 20262. Effective retroactively for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, Bill C-15 doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% refundable investment tax credit from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000, thereby raising the maximum annual federal cash refund from $1,050,000 to $2,100,0001. Concurrently, the legislation broadened the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from the historical $10,000,000–$50,000,000 corridor to a wider $15,000,000–$75,000,000 range, extended the enhanced 35% refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) for the first time, and reinstated the eligibility of capital expenditures and capital lease costs for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 20241. Complementing these statutory enhancements, the CRA implemented an elective Pre-Claim Approval process on April 1, 2026, designed to provide upfront technical eligibility determinations within eight weeks and halve expenditure review processing times from 180 calendar days to 90 calendar days1.

body.text: The Canadian SR&ED system operates through a distinct two-stage statutory mechanism that separates expenditure deductibility from tax credit generation6. First, under Subsection 37(1) of the Income Tax Act, a taxpayer carrying on business in Canada may pool allowable current and (post-December 15, 2024) capital SR&ED expenditures to deduct them in full against current-year income from business or carry them forward indefinitely into future taxation years6. Second, under Section 127 and Section 127.1 of the Income Tax Act, the taxpayer earns an Investment Tax Credit calculated as a percentage (35% or 15%) of its "qualified SR&ED expenditures"2. To prevent double-dipping between tax deductions and tax credits, any federal ITC claimed in a given taxation year (whether refunded in cash or applied against Part I tax payable) is recaptured into the taxpayer's income or deducted from the Section 37 expenditure pool in the immediately following taxation year, while provincial R&D tax credits constitute "government assistance" that reduces the federal qualified expenditure base in the current year19. From a macro-fiscal perspective, this two-tier interaction lowers the after-tax marginal cost of R&D capital and labour while ensuring that statutory tax relief scales proportionally with net out-of-pocket technical risk1.
Federal Statutory Framework and the Landmark Bill C-15 Legislative Reforms
Statutory Architecture of the Income Tax Act and Regulations

The legal authority governing federal R&D tax incentives rests on four interconnected pillars of the Income Tax Act and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations4. The first pillar is the definitional gatekeeper codified in Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, which establishes the exhaustive legal definition of "scientific research and experimental development" that applies uniformly across federal and harmonised provincial tax statutes3. Subsection 248(1) also defines pivotal structural terms that control claimant eligibility and expenditure caps, including "Canadian-controlled private corporation" (CCPC), "salary or wages" (defined as income from an office or employment as computed under Sections 5 to 8 of the Act), "specified shareholder" (a taxpayer who owns, directly or indirectly, at any time in the year, at least 10% of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation), and "specified employee" (an employee who is a specified shareholder of the employer or does not deal at arm's length with the employer)5.

The second statutory pillar governs expenditure pooling and deductibility under Section 37 of the Income Tax Act5. Paragraph 37(1)(a) encompasses current expenditures on SR&ED carried on in Canada directly by the taxpayer or on its behalf, whereas Paragraph 37(1)(b)—reinstated by Bill C-15 for property acquired after December 15, 2024—governs capital expenditures on depreciable property intended for all or substantially all (90% or more) use or value consumption in SR&ED in Canada11. Recognizing that domestic research projects occasionally require limited testing or technical execution abroad, Subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5) permit a restricted inclusion of salaries and wages for SR&ED carried on outside Canada by Canadian-resident employees, capped strictly at 10% of total salaries and wages paid for SR&ED carried on in Canada15. Within the same section, Subsections 37(8), 37(9), and 37(9.1) impose specific allocation rules and statutory ceilings on employee and specified employee compensation, while Subsection 37(11) codifies the absolute 18-month filing bar for prescribed forms5.

The third pillar resides in Section 2900 of the Income Tax Regulations, which defines the precise parameters of directly engaged labour, overhead and other expenditures under the Traditional Method, and the calculation of the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) under Subsection 2900(4)4. Subsections 2900(7) through 2900(10) enforce strict caps and exclusions on the salary base used to compute the 55% notional overhead proxy, particularly for specified employees employed across associated corporate groups4. The fourth pillar comprises Sections 127 and 127.1 of the Income Tax Act5. Section 127 defines "qualified expenditure" under Subsection 127(9), establishes the basic 15% ITC rate, and sets forth the enhanced 35% ITC rate under Subsection 127(10.1), the $6,000,000 expenditure limit under Subsection 127(10.2), and mandatory allocation rules among associated corporations under Subsection 127(10.3)2. Section 127.1 then governs the cash refundability of ITCs earned by "qualifying corporations" and unincorporated businesses, subject to the qualifying income limit and taxable capital phase-out rules5.
Detailed Analysis of the Bill C-15 (2025–2026) Reforms

The enactment of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026 fundamentally recalibrated the economics of R&D investment in Canada for all taxation years commencing on or after December 16, 20241. Tax practitioners and corporate claimants must account for five structural transformations introduced by the legislation and their broader strategic implications for corporate finance and capital allocation1.

First, Parliament doubled the enhanced expenditure limit under amended Subsection 127(10.2), raising the baseline annual expenditure ceiling eligible for the enhanced 35% ITC rate from $3,000,000 to $6,000,00011. Because current qualified SR&ED expenditures within the expenditure limit are 100% refundable for eligible corporations, the maximum annual federal cash refund available to an associated corporate group doubled from $1,050,000 to $2,100,0001. This reform directly redresses decade-long wage and hardware cost inflation that had steadily eroded the real purchasing power of the legacy $3,000,000 cap, which previously forced scaling technology companies into the 15% non-refundable tier once their engineering headcount exceeded approximately 20 to 25 full-time researchers2.

Second, Bill C-15 expanded the taxable capital phase-out corridor and introduced an elective gross revenue alternative1. Under the pre-reform rules, a CCPC's $3,000,000 expenditure limit began to phase out once the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada of the corporation and its associated corporations exceeded $10,000,000, reaching zero at $50,000,0001. Because taxable capital employed in Canada (computed on T2 Schedule 33, Line 690) includes share capital, contributed surplus, retained earnings, and certain debt instruments, venture-backed technology and life sciences startups frequently lost access to the enhanced 35% refundable credit immediately after closing Series B or Series C equity financings, despite remaining pre-revenue or unprofitable14. Bill C-15 raised the phase-out floor to $15,000,000 and the ceiling to $75,000,000, and introduced an elective alternative test allowing claimants to phase out the expenditure limit based on average gross revenue over the three preceding taxation years across the same $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 corridor1. This structural decoupling ensures that balance-sheet equity raised to fund multi-year clinical trials or deep-tech hardware development no longer triggers a punitive clawback of refundable R&D support1.

Third, the legislation extended the enhanced 35% refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs)1. Historically, a corporation that listed its shares on a designated stock exchange (such as the Toronto Stock Exchange or TSX Venture Exchange) ceased to be a CCPC and immediately forfeited both the 35% enhanced rate and cash refundability, dropping to the 15% non-refundable basic rate1. Under Bill C-15, Eligible Canadian Public Corporations—resident public corporations that are not controlled directly or indirectly by one or more non-resident persons—are granted access to the 35% enhanced refundable ITC on up to $6,000,000 of qualified expenditures, with their expenditure limit phased out linearly based on their three-year average gross revenue between $15,000,000 and $75,000,0001. By eliminating the "IPO penalty" for domestic public companies, the reform removes a major tax distortion that previously discouraged Canadian life sciences, clean-tech, and mining-technology firms from accessing domestic public equity markets1.

Fourth, Bill C-15 restored the eligibility of capital expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and capital lease costs1. Between January 1, 2014 and December 15, 2024, capital expenditures and capital lease payments were entirely excluded from SR&ED deductibility and ITC calculations1. For depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024 (and lease costs first becoming payable after December 15, 2024), Bill C-15 restored the pre-2014 capital rules11. This restoration allows capital-intensive sectors—including artificial intelligence companies acquiring high-performance GPU compute clusters, advanced manufacturers, semiconductor fabricators, and biotechnology laboratories—to claim both Section 37 deductions and ITCs on qualifying machinery and equipment1. Capital expenditures earning the enhanced 35% ITC are refundable at a statutory rate of 40%, producing an immediate 14% cash refund on capital outlay with the remaining 21% credit available to offset Part I tax or carry forward for 20 years11.

Fifth, the legislative expansion was paired with comprehensive administrative modernisation and the launch of Pre-Claim Approval2. Between April and October 2026, the CRA updated its entire suite of SR&ED administrative forms and policy instruments—including Form T661 (Version 26, May 15, 2026), Form T1145 (May 15, 2026), Form T1146 (May 15, 2026), T2 Schedule 31 (May 22, 2026), T2 Schedule 49 (May 29, 2026), the Shared-Use-Equipment Policy (May 22, 2026), the Total Qualified Expenditure Policy (May 22, 2026), the Lease Expenditures Policy (June 8, 2026), the Capital Expenditures Policy (June 29, 2026), and the SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy (October 7, 2026)—and launched its optional Pre-Claim Approval process on April 1, 20262.
Scientific and Technological Eligibility Criteria and Judicial Precedents
The Statutory Three-Branch Definition under Subsection 248(1)

Under Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, "scientific research and experimental development" means a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis3. The statutory definition bifurcates eligible core work into three distinct branches, supplemented by a fourth category for eligible support work3. Basic research, codified under Paragraph (a), comprises work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view18. Applied research, codified under Paragraph (b), encompasses work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view18. Experimental development, codified under Paragraph (c), covers work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto3. In Canadian audit practice, the vast majority of corporate SR&ED claims are filed under Paragraph (c) as experimental development, where even modest, incremental improvements to existing industrial processes qualify provided they seek to resolve genuine technological uncertainty3.

To ensure that ancillary engineering activities necessary to execute experiments are not artificially severed from core research, Paragraph 248(1)(d) incorporates eligible support work into the statutory definition18. Under Paragraph (d), work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research qualifies as SR&ED where that work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of core basic research, applied research, or experimental development described in Paragraph (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer1. Conversely, Subsection 248(1) expressly excludes routine and commercial activities from the definition of SR&ED, even if they involve highly skilled technical personnel. Statutory exclusions encompass market research or sales promotion; quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; research in the social sciences or the humanities; prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process; style changes; and routine data collection.
The Five-Question Common-Law Test: Northwest Hydraulic and C.W. Agencies

While Subsection 248(1) supplies the statutory text, its authoritative legal interpretation was established by Judge Donald Bowman (later Chief Justice of the Tax Court of Canada) in the landmark decision Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, 1998 CanLII 553 (TCC), [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 98 DTC 18393. At paragraph 16 of Northwest Hydraulic, Judge Bowman articulated the five foundational criteria—subsequently adopted verbatim as binding appellate law by the Federal Court of Appeal in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2001 FCA 393, [2002] 1 C.T.C. 212, 2002 DTC 6740 (at paragraph 17)—that Canadian courts apply to determine whether a claimed activity constitutes SR&ED3.

The first criterion asks whether there was a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures3. If the resolution of a technical problem is reasonably predictable using established techniques, publicly available documentation, or standard procedures known to competent professionals in the relevant field, no technological uncertainty exists3. Crucially, Judge Bowman recognized in Northwest Hydraulic that technological uncertainty can arise at the system integration level—even when individual components are well known—if their interaction creates unpredictable behaviour, and he further recognized that "shop floor SR&ED" may occur during industrial design when abnormal testing efforts are required to overcome knowledge gaps absent from the public domain29.

The second criterion asks whether the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty3. In judicial and administrative application, this entails a structured five-stage iterative process: the observation of the subject matter of the problem; the formulation of a clear technical objective; the identification and articulation of the underlying technological uncertainty; the formulation of a testable hypothesis or hypotheses designed to reduce or eliminate that uncertainty; and the methodical determination of an experimental or analytical procedure to test the hypothesis3.

The third criterion asks whether the procedure adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of the hypotheses3. As Justice Sommerfeldt explained in Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 6 (at paragraph 33), the scientific method is characterized by trained and systematic observation, measurement, and experimentation, whereby variables are controlled or systematically varied so that an independent professional can trace the logical progression between the premise of an experiment and its empirical result3. Unguided trial-and-error tinkering or random parameter adjustments fail this requirement3.

The fourth criterion asks whether the process resulted in a technological advancement—that is to say, an advancement in the general understanding of scientific relations or technology3. In a commercial business context, this means that when a new or improved product or process is created, it must embody a scientific or technological advancement that expands the knowledge base of the company's technical staff beyond standard practice29. Crucially, an SR&ED project does not need to succeed commercially or even achieve its practical engineering objective to yield a qualifying technological advancement; the definitive falsification or rejection of a plausible hypothesis through rigorous experimentation advances technological knowledge by establishing why a specific technical approach fails under defined boundary conditions34.

The fifth criterion asks whether a detailed record of the hypotheses, tests, and results was kept as the work progressed3. As Judge Bowman observed in Northwest Hydraulic (at paragraph 16), although the Income Tax Act and the Income Tax Regulations do not state so explicitly, it is self-evident that a detailed record of the hypotheses, tests, and results must be kept contemporaneously as the investigation unfolds in order to substantiate that a systematic scientific investigation actually occurred6.
Administrative Guidelines vs. Binding Jurisprudence (2021–2026 Case Law)

In August 2021, the CRA archived its legacy Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy and published revised administrative guidelines structured around a simplified two-part "Why and How" framework6. Under this administrative formulation, the "Why" requirement asks why the work was conducted in order to advance scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving technological advancement, while the "How" requirement asks how the work was conducted by means of a systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis—specifically looking for the generation of an idea or hypothesis consistent with known facts, the testing of that hypothesis by experiment or analysis, the development of logical conclusions based on the findings, and the keeping of progressive evidence6.

Following the release of the 2021 guidelines, several taxpayers argued before the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) and the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA) that the CRA's administrative restatement had relaxed or replaced the strict common-law requirements of Northwest Hydraulic6. Between 2021 and 2026, Canadian appellate and trial courts decisively rejected that contention, reinforcing the binding primacy of the five Northwest Hydraulic questions while clarifying how they apply to modern applied engineering, food science, construction, and software development contexts6.

body.text: Several critical second- and third-order audit principles emerge from this jurisprudence that directly govern how technical narratives and evidentiary files must be constructed. First, as Chief Justice Rossiter emphasized in 2023 TCC 108 (at paragraph 89), "the lacking knowledge must exist in the base of scientific or technological knowledge, not simply be unknown to the claimant"3. Consequently, a taxpayer cannot claim SR&ED merely because its internal engineers are unfamiliar with an established software framework or are configuring off-the-shelf equipment without encountering an objective limitation in the underlying technology3. Second, in 6398316 Canada Inc. v. The Queen (2021 TCC 17), Justice Lafleur clarified the delicate boundary between economic constraints and technological uncertainty: while purely financial risk never constitutes SR&ED, business and cost constraints imposed by the claimant's commercial context can frame the boundaries of a project, provided the claimant formulates hypotheses that resolve genuine technological obstacles rather than merely shopping for cheaper materials39.

Third, National R&D Inc. v. Canada (2022 FCA 72; affirming 2020 TCC 47) and Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada (2021 FCA 88) establish beyond doubt that administrative guidelines published by the CRA cannot dilute statutory criteria interpreted by the courts6. Writing for the Federal Court of Appeal in National R&D, Justice Rennie affirmed that the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria remain the mandatory legal test for Subsection 248(1), upheld the trial judge's rejection of records that were "vague," "unclear," and failed to show a logical progression between experimental premise and result, and warned litigants that expert witness reports that opine directly on the ultimate legal question of whether work constitutes SR&ED (rather than explaining the state of the art and technical uncertainties) risk being ruled inadmissible22.

Fourth, the December 2024 decision of Justice J. Scott Bodie in Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King (2024 TCC 159, amended January 17, 2025) illustrates how small and medium-sized enterprises can prevail against overly rigid CRA technical denials3. In Manning Canning, the taxpayer sought to create a vinegar-based drink containing unpasteurized cold-pressed fruit juice ("Chrisoda") that could remain shelf-stable in aluminum cans at room temperature for at least two years without heat treatment or glass bottling, after initial production runs caused cans to explode due to microbial oxygen release3. The Minister denied the claim on the grounds that refrigeration and heat pasteurization were well-known preservation methods and that the taxpayer tested commercially available preservatives including potassium sorbate, sodium benzoate, and Chiber3. Justice Bodie rejected the Minister's characterization of the project objective, holding that testing the mushroom-derived preservative Chiber outside its known dairy application in an unpasteurized cold-pressed juice matrix was not routine engineering3. Because the taxpayer formulated clear hypotheses, conducted systematic trials measuring quantitative parameters (such as pH and microbial counts), and cited Justice Jorré's principle in 2014 TCC 313 (at paragraph 94) that contemporaneous documents do not require a specific legal format so long as progressive records resolve factual disputes, the Tax Court allowed the appeal in full3.
Qualifying Expenditure Mechanics, Overhead Elections, and Specified Employee Restrictions

To convert eligible scientific or technological activities into tax deductions under Section 37 and Investment Tax Credits under Section 127, a claimant must accurately classify, prorate, and cap its expenditures across Part 3, Part 4, and Part 5 of Form T66115.
Salaries and Wages: Direct Labour, Support Staff, and Foreign Permissible Wages

Under Subsection 37(8) of the Income Tax Act and Paragraph 2900(2)(b) of the Income Tax Regulations, deductible SR&ED salaries and wages encompass compensation paid to employees for the portion of their working time they are "directly engaged" in the prosecution of SR&ED5. Directly engaged activities include hands-on experimentation, prototype fabrication, coding experimental algorithms, analysing test data, direct first-line technical supervision of SR&ED staff, and eligible Paragraph 248(1)(d) support work1. General administrative, executive, legal, marketing, and human resources personnel are not directly engaged in SR&ED; their compensation cannot be claimed on Line 300 or Line 305 of Form T661, though certain directly related and incremental clerical or maintenance support may be captured if the claimant elects the Traditional Overhead Method11.

Where an employee spends "all or substantially all" (defined by the CRA as 90% or more) of their employment time in a taxation year directly engaged in SR&ED, 100% of their eligible salary or wages may be included in the SR&ED claim, provided the claimant maintains specific contemporaneous evidence substantiating that 90%+ allocation—a requirement that the CRA enforces rigorously for company founders, who often perform unrecorded commercial, fundraising, and corporate governance duties5. Employees spending less than 90% of their time on SR&ED must have their salaries prorated strictly according to the ratio of hours spent directly on eligible SR&ED to total hours worked in the taxation year5.

While SR&ED must generally be carried on within Canada, Subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5) permit a claimant to include salaries and wages paid to Canadian-resident employees performing SR&ED outside Canada (reported on Line 307 for non-specified employees and Line 309 for specified employees of Form T661), provided the foreign work is directly undertaken by the taxpayer rather than subcontracted, is integral to a core Canadian SR&ED project, and the combined foreign salaries on Lines 307 and 309 do not exceed 10% of the total salaries and wages claimed for SR&ED performed in Canada on Lines 300 and 30515.
Specified Employee Restrictions and 2023–2026 YMPE / YAMPE Thresholds

The Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations impose stringent anti-avoidance restrictions on compensation paid to a "specified employee"—defined in Subsection 248(1) as an employee who is a "specified shareholder" (owning, directly or indirectly, at any time in the taxation year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation, counting shares held by non-arm's-length persons) or who does not deal at arm's length with the employer (such as a spouse, child, or sibling of a controlling shareholder, even if that family member owns zero shares)5. Because share ownership at any time in the year triggers specified shareholder status, a startup founder whose equity stake is diluted below 10% partway through a taxation year during a venture capital financing round remains a specified employee for that entire taxation year5.

Specified employees are subject to three mandatory statutory restrictions designed to prevent closely held corporations from disguising dividend distributions as tax-subsidised R&D wages4. First, under Subsection 37(9) of the Income Tax Act (and Guide T4088, Line 305), remuneration based on profits or a bonus—defined by the CRA Salary or Wages Policy as any amount paid in addition to normal base pay—paid to a specified employee is strictly excluded from SR&ED expenditures5. Second, under Subsection 37(9.1) of the Income Tax Act, the maximum direct SR&ED salary or wages that may be claimed on Line 305 of Form T661 for a specified employee cannot exceed 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under Section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year that the individual was a specified employee4: 5 × YMPE × D ÷ 365, where D is the number of days in the taxation year on which the individual was a specified employee.

Third, under Subsection 2900(7) of the Income Tax Regulations, the amount of a specified employee's salary that may enter the salary base in Part 5 of Form T661 (to earn the 55% overhead proxy) is restricted to the lesser of 75% of the specified employee's total salary or wages for the year (both SR&ED and non-SR&ED, excluding bonuses, profit-based remuneration, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages paid in the year) and 2.5 times the YMPE, prorated by the total number of days in the taxation year that the claimant employed the individual4: 2.5 × YMPE × D ÷ 365, where D is the number of days in the taxation year in which the individual was an employee of the claimant.

A critical technical distinction exists between Subsection 37(9.1) and Subsection 2900(7) that frequently trips up corporate tax preparers: while the 5 × YMPE direct wage cap is prorated by the number of days the individual was a specified employee, the 2.5 × YMPE proxy salary base cap is prorated strictly by the number of days the individual was employed in the year, with no proration for any portion of the year during which the employee was not a specified employee4. Furthermore, under Subsections 2900(8) and 2900(10) of the Income Tax Regulations, if a specified employee is employed by two or more associated corporations (including individuals related to the corporation or partnerships with related or associated partners, which are deemed to be associated corporations for this purpose) in taxation years ending in the same calendar year, the 2.5 × YMPE proxy salary base ceiling must be shared across the associated group, such that the claimant's maximum inclusion is 2.5 × YMPE minus the amount included by the associated corporation4.

Beginning January 1, 2024, the Canada Pension Plan Enhancement introduced a two-tier earnings ceiling architecture: the first earnings ceiling remains the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE), subject to base and first additional CPP contributions of 5.95% each for employers and employees (5.75% each from January 1, 2027) above the $3,500 basic exemption; the second earnings ceiling is the Year's Additional Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YAMPE, set at approximately 7% above the YMPE in 2024 and 14% above the YMPE in 2025 and subsequent years), subject to second additional CPP contributions (CPP2) at 4.00% each for employers and employees (8.00% for self-employed individuals, reported in Box 16A or Box 17A on T4 slips)43. For SR&ED purposes, while the employer's matching CPP and CPP2 contributions are statutory payroll outlays, the statutory caps under ITA Subsection 37(9.1) and ITR Subsection 2900(7) remain anchored exclusively to the first ceiling (YMPE under Section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan), not the YAMPE4.

The direct SR&ED salary claimed on Line 305 for each founder is $70,000, which sits well below the $373,000 ceiling5. For the Part 5 PPA salary base, each founder's inclusion is the lesser of $70,000 (actual SR&ED salary), $75,000 (75% of total $100,000 salary), and $186,500 (2.5 × $74,600), resulting in a $70,000 proxy base and a $38,500 PPA (55% × $70,000), generating $108,500 of qualified expenditures and $37,975 in refundable federal ITC per founder at the 35% rate5. Conversely, if an owner-manager draws a $250,000 base salary and devotes 100% of their time to SR&ED in 2026, the direct SR&ED salary on Line 305 is $250,000, but because 75% of total salary ($187,500) exceeds 2.5 × YMPE ($186,500), the Part 5 proxy salary base is capped at $186,500, generating a maximum PPA of $102,57515.
Overhead Calculation Methods: Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) vs. Traditional Method

On Line 160 or Line 162 of Part 3 of Form T661, a claimant must elect to compute its SR&ED overhead using either the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Method or the Traditional Method15. This election is irrevocable for the taxation year once Form T661 is filed; a taxpayer may switch methods from one taxation year to the next, but cannot amend a filed return to switch between the proxy and traditional methods for the same taxation year15.

Under the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Method, the claimant foregoes claiming specific overhead outlays (such as shop supplies, utilities, property taxes, or indirect support labour) within its SR&ED claim; instead, those actual expenses remain deductible as ordinary business expenses under Section 9 of the Income Tax Act1. In their place, the claimant computes a notional overhead amount equal to 55% of its eligible SR&ED salary base under Subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations11. Under Paragraph 2900(9)(a), the salary base comprises the salaries and wages of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada (Lines 300 and 305), strictly excluding taxable benefits (such as employer-paid group health plans or automobile benefits), bonuses, remuneration based on profits, and prior years' unpaid salaries paid in the year, while remaining subject to the specified employee caps under Subsections 2900(7) and 2900(8)4. The resulting PPA is entered in Part 5 and added to Part 4 to generate Investment Tax Credits, though it never enters the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool11. Tax practitioners must note that a frequent error in unverified secondary commentary is citing a 65% proxy rate; the statutory PPA rate was 65% up to 2012, transitioned to 60% for 2013, and has stood at 55% since January 1, 201411.

Under the Traditional Method, the claimant calculates no notional proxy amount; instead, it itemises and claims actual overhead and other expenditures on Line 360 of Form T66111. To qualify under the Traditional Method, every overhead expenditure must satisfy a strict two-prong legal test: it must be directly related to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada, and incremental (meaning the cost would not have been incurred by the business but for the execution of the SR&ED activities)11. While the PPA method is overwhelmingly favoured by software, artificial intelligence, data analytics, and engineering firms due to its low administrative burden and generous 55% yield on direct salaries, the Traditional Method can be financially superior for facility-intensive manufacturers, metallurgical processors, or companies that rely heavily on specified employees (whose proxy base is capped at $186,500) or subcontractors (which generate zero PPA)1.
Materials, Subcontractors, and Restored Capital & Lease Expenditures

Beyond direct labour and overhead, Part 3 and Part 4 of Form T661 govern materials, third-party contracts, and restored capital and lease expenditures11. For materials, claimants may include 100% of the cost of physical materials that are either consumed (rendered virtually worthless or destroyed during testing, such as chemical reagents or destructive test coupons) or transformed (incorporated into an experimental prototype or pilot plant during the prosecution of SR&ED)11. The eligible cost of materials includes the invoice price, customs and excise duties, freight, and storage directly attributable to those materials11. However, if an experimental prototype or transformed material is subsequently sold commercially or converted to commercial use, the SR&ED recapture rules claw back the lesser of the proceeds of disposition (or fair market value at conversion) and the original cost claimed, adding the recaptured ITC directly to Part I tax payable19.

Where a claimant contracts out eligible SR&ED work to an arm's-length Canadian taxable supplier that performs the work in Canada on the claimant's behalf, 100% of the eligible contract payment is deductible in the Section 37 pool, but only 80% of the contract payment is included in qualified SR&ED expenditures for ITC calculation purposes (removing 20% to strip out the contractor's assumed profit markup)11. Payments for contractor work performed outside Canada are completely ineligible for SR&ED11. Where an SR&ED contract is executed between non-arm's-length parties, no 80% haircut applies, but the payer cannot claim ITCs on the contract payments directly; instead, the non-arm's-length performer incurs the underlying expenditures and the parties may execute Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length, reported on Line 540 of Form T661) to transfer the qualified expenditures to the payer, excluding any expenditures on depreciable property acquired before December 16, 202413. Payments to approved universities, colleges, research institutes, or research consortia for SR&ED related to the taxpayer's business class of operations also qualify at the 80% inclusion rate.

Under Bill C-15 and Version 26 of Form T661 (updated May 15, 2026), depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024 (and lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024) are eligible across three distinct statutory pathways11. The first pathway covers All or Substantially All (ASA) Capital Property claimed on Line 390 of Form T66113. This encompasses new or used depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024 that the claimant intended at acquisition to use all or substantially all (90% or more) of its operating time over its expected useful life in SR&ED in Canada, or to have 90% or more of its value consumed in SR&ED in Canada11. Land, buildings, leasehold interests in buildings, goodwill, and inventory remain excluded11. The full capital cost—comprising purchase price, installation costs, customs and excise duties, transportation, and other acquisition costs—is claimed on Line 390 (and must therefore be omitted from regular Capital Cost Allowance on Schedule T2SCH8), entering both the Section 37 pool on Line 400 and Part 4 qualified capital expenditures on Line 55813.

The second pathway governs Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) claimed on Line 504 (and Box 792) of Form T66113. When new depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024 is used primarily (more than 50% but less than 90% of its operating time) in SR&ED in Canada, the SR&ED ITC calculation is identical under both the PPA and Traditional methods: the claimant includes 25% of the capital cost of the equipment on Line 504 in the first period (first-term SUE) and the other 25% in the second period (second-term SUE), yielding a combined 50% qualified expenditure inclusion across the two periods13. Unlike ASA capital property on Line 390, the capital cost of Shared-Use Equipment does not enter the Section 37 deductible SR&ED expenditure pool; instead, the claimant depreciates the capital cost under regular Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) rates and rules on Schedule T2SCH813.

The third pathway restores Equipment Lease Costs incurred after December 15, 202413. Lease payments for equipment used 90% or more (ASA) in SR&ED are 100% claimable under both overhead methods, excluding general office equipment or furniture when using the proxy method13. For leased equipment used primarily (50% to under 90%) in SR&ED, a claimant electing the PPA method may claim 50% (half) of the lease costs on Line 355 of Form T66115. Conversely, a claimant electing the Traditional Method may claim the SR&ED-allocable portion of lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024 for equipment used less than 90% of the time in SR&ED directly on Line 360 as overhead and other expenditures13.

Claimant Categories, Credit Rates, and Refundability Rules

Under Sections 127 and 127.1 of the Income Tax Act (as amended by Bill C-15 for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024), the federal SR&ED ITC rate and cash refundability depend on the legal classification of the claimant and whether the qualified expenditures fall within the corporation's annual expenditure limit2.

Qualifying Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) earn the enhanced 35% ITC rate on up to $6,000,000 of qualified SR&ED expenditures within their annual expenditure limit1. For a CCPC that satisfies the definition of a "qualifying corporation" under Subsection 127.1(2), the 35% credit is 100% refundable on qualified current expenditures (yielding up to $2,100,000 in annual cash refunds) and 40% refundable on qualified capital expenditures (yielding a 14% immediate cash refund and 21% non-refundable credit)5. If a CCPC's prior-year taxable income exceeded its "qualifying income limit" (determined under Subsection 127.1(2) and reduced when prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada of the associated group passes $15,000,000), the 35% ITC earned within the remaining expenditure limit is 40% refundable on both current and capital expenditures5.

Under the Bill C-15 expansion, Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs)—resident public corporations not controlled by non-residents—now also earn the enhanced 35% refundable ITC on up to $6,000,000 of qualified expenditures (100% refundable on current expenditures and 40% refundable on capital expenditures), subject to the three-year average gross revenue phase-out between $15,000,000 and $75,000,0001. For both CCPCs and ECPCs, any qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred above the $6,000,000 expenditure limit (or above a reduced expenditure limit resulting from the phase-out) earn the basic 15% ITC rate2. For a qualifying corporation whose prior-year taxable income did not exceed its qualifying income limit, the 15% ITC on current expenditures above the limit is 40% refundable (producing a 6% cash refund and 9% non-refundable credit); otherwise, the 15% ITC is completely non-refundable34.

Foreign-controlled corporations (such as Canadian subsidiaries of United States, European, or Asian parent corporations) and public corporations exceeding the $75,000,000 revenue threshold earn the basic 15% non-refundable ITC on all qualified SR&ED expenditures, with no upper expenditure limit2. Finally, unincorporated businesses, sole proprietors, individual partners, and certain trusts (claiming credits on Form T2038(IND)) earn the basic 15% ITC rate, which is 40% refundable after offsetting federal tax payable2. Across all claimant categories, any non-refundable portion of an SR&ED Investment Tax Credit may be carried back 3 taxation years or carried forward 20 taxation years to offset federal Part I income tax payable19.
Expenditure Limit Phase-Out Mathematics ($15M to $75M Corridor)

For taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, the $6,000,000 enhanced expenditure limit for an associated corporate group is reduced linearly as prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada (or, by election or for ECPCs, three-year average gross revenue) increases from $15,000,000 to $75,000,0001. Where total prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada (or three-year average gross revenue) of the corporation and all associated corporations exceeds $15,000,000 across the $60,000,000 phase-out band, the annual Expenditure Limit (EL) prorated for a taxation year of D days is governed by the formula2: EL = $6,000,000 × ($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000 × D ÷ 365, where A is the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which that prior-year amount exceeds $15,000,000.

Equivalently, every $10 of prior-year taxable capital (or three-year average gross revenue) above $15,000,000 reduces the $6,000,000 expenditure limit by $1 (a 10% reduction rate), until the enhanced expenditure limit is completely eliminated at $75,000,0002. Under Subsection 127(10.3) of the Income Tax Act, associated corporations must share this single expenditure limit by filing an executed allocation agreement on T2 Schedule 49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit)11. Ignoring the corporate association rules under Section 256 of the Income Tax Act is one of the costliest structural compliance failures in Canadian tax practice, as undisclosed association across venture portfolios or family trusts triggers retroactive reassessment of the 35% enhanced rate down to the 15% non-refundable rate11.
Unpaid Amounts (Subsection 78(4)) and Government Assistance Grind-Down (Subsection 127(9))

Two statutory adjustment rules in Part 4 of Form T661 routinely trigger audit reassessments if misapplied during year-end financial close5. First, under Subsection 78(4) of the Income Tax Act, any salary, wages, or other remuneration accrued at the end of a taxation year that remains unpaid on the day that is 180 days after the end of that taxation year is deemed not to have been incurred in the taxation year; instead, it is deemed to be incurred only in the subsequent taxation year in which it is actually paid, for both Section 37 deduction and Section 127 ITC purposes5. Similarly, current SR&ED expenditures other than salary or wages (such as accrued subcontractor invoices or material purchases) that remain unpaid 180 days after the end of the taxation year must be deducted from qualified SR&ED expenditures on Line 528 of Form T661, and can only be included when subsequently paid17.

Second, under Subsection 127(9) and Paragraph 37(1)(d) of the Income Tax Act, both the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool and Part 4 qualified SR&ED expenditures (on Line 513 of Form T661) must be reduced by the amount of any "government assistance" or "non-government assistance" (as well as contract payments received for performing SR&ED for another party) that the taxpayer has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive in respect of the SR&ED at the time of filing19. Government assistance encompasses direct innovation grants (such as NRC IRAP contributions, Strategic Innovation Fund grants, or provincial Alberta Innovates grants) as well as all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits19. If a taxpayer subsequently repays government assistance that previously reduced its qualified expenditures (for example, repaying a conditionally repayable government contribution), the repayment is added back to qualified expenditures on Line 560 of Form T661 in the year of repayment19. Where non-arm's-length parties share government assistance, they may file Form T1145 (Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length)13.
Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes: Followers and Holdouts After Bill C-15

Across Canada, nine provinces and one territory offer dedicated R&D tax credits that stack alongside the federal SR&ED programme, leaving only Prince Edward Island, the Northwest Territories, and Nunavut without a standalone provincial or territorial R&D tax credit8. Except for Québec (administered independently by Revenu Québec on the CO-17 corporate return) and Alberta (administered independently by Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration on the AT1 corporate return), all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits are administered directly by the CRA through schedules attached to the federal T2 Corporation Income Tax Return and reported on T2 Schedule 5 (Tax Calculation Supplementary – Corporations)19.

Following the Royal Assent of federal Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, a pronounced fiscal divergence emerged across provincial capitals between "Followers"—such as British Columbia, which expressly harmonised its provincial rules with the new federal $15,000,000–$75,000,000 phase-out, ECPC eligibility, and capital expenditure restoration—and "Holdouts"—such as Ontario, which retained its $3,000,000 expenditure cap for the OITC while adopting post-December 15, 2024 capital expenditures, and Alberta, which modified AT1 Schedule 29 to exclude restored federal capital expenditures from the Alberta IEG base7.

body.text: Deep-Dive Analysis of Key Provincial Jurisdictions
Ontario (OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC)

Under Section 96 of the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), a qualifying CCPC with a permanent establishment in Ontario may claim the 8% refundable Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC) on T2 Schedule 566 (entered on Line 468 of Schedule 5), alongside the 3.5% non-refundable Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC) on T2 Schedule 5087. While Ontario updated its OITC definition of qualified expenditures to include 100% of qualified capital expenditures made on or after December 16, 2024 (reversing the January 1, 2014 to December 15, 2024 capital exclusion, whereas pre-2014 capital expenditures were included at 40%), Ontario explicitly declined to adopt the federal $6,000,000 expenditure limit7. Consequently, the OITC remains subject to its own independent $3,000,000 annual expenditure limit (yielding a maximum $240,000 refundable credit per associated group), which phases out when prior-year federal taxable income lies between $500,000 and $800,000 or when prior-year specified capital lies between $25,000,000 and $50,000,0007. Under Subsection 96(14) of the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario) (and corresponding ORDTC waiver provisions), a corporation may elect to waive all or part of its current-year tax credit—a critical planning tool frequently exercised by unprofitable startups to avoid grinding down their 35% refundable federal SR&ED ITC base on Line 513 with a 3.5% non-refundable ORDTC that cannot yet be absorbed against Ontario corporate income tax19.
Québec (Revenu Québec RD-1029.7-V and the New Post-March 25, 2025 CRIC Regime on Form RD-1029.8.CR)

Québec operates the most autonomous R&D tax incentive system in Canada, administered by Revenu Québec (guided by publication IN-109-V, Tax Assistance for Scientific Research and Experimental Development) and requiring a separate provincial corporate return (CO-17) along with Form RD-222-V (Deduction Respecting Scientific Research and Experimental Development Expenditures)34. Unlike the federal system, Québec does not use a 55% notional overhead proxy; instead, for taxation years beginning on or before March 25, 2025, Québec structured its primary incentive around the refundable Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D) (claimed on Form RD-1029.7-V and allocated among associated corporations via Form RD-1029.7.8), which provided a base rate of 14% and an enhanced rate of up to 30% on the first $3,000,000 of eligible Québec R&D salaries and 50% of arm's-length Québec subcontractor payments above a statutory exclusion threshold, complemented by distinct credits for university or public research centre contracts (Form RD-1029.8.6-V), private partnership pre-competitive research (Form RD-1029.8.16.1-V, requiring a qualification certificate from the Minister of Economy, Innovation and Energy), and research consortium fees (Form RD-1029.8.9.03-V)34.

For all taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, Québec enacted a sweeping modernisation of its R&D tax architecture by introducing the refundable Tax Credit for R&D and Pre-Commercialization (CRIC), claimed on the newly released Form RD-1029.8.CR53. The CRIC replaces Form RD-1029.7 and consolidates the former university, pre-competitive partnership, and consortium R&D credits into a single unified refundable credit covering both R&D and eligible pre-commercialization activities (such as regulatory testing, industrial design, and pre-production validation) as well as eligible capital property acquired for R&D or pre-commercialization in Québec53. Furthermore, Québec technology companies developing interactive digital products or video games frequently combine federal SR&ED (35%) and Québec R&D tax credits (14%–30%) with the Québec Multimedia Tax Credit (26.25%–37.5% refundable)—achieving net cash recovery exceeding 50% to 70% of eligible R&D outlays while ensuring no single expenditure dollar is double-counted across mutually exclusive provincial bases34.
Alberta (Innovation Employment Grant — AT1 Schedule 29 and the Post-Bill C-15 Line 557 Rule)

Effective January 1, 2021, Alberta established the Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) under Sections 26.95 to 26.99 (Division 7 of Part 6) of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act (detailed in Information Circular IEG-1), claimed on AT1 Schedule 29 (Form AT29) and Form AT4970 (Listing of Innovation Employment Grant Projects Claimed in Alberta) within 15 months after the AT1 filing due date19. The IEG employs a two-tier incremental formula on up to $4,000,000 of annual eligible Alberta R&D expenditures (yielding a maximum annual refundable grant of $800,000, reported on Line 134 of Form AT29 and Line 129 of the AT1 return)8. Under Tier 1 (Part I calculation on Line 110 of Form AT29), every dollar of current-year eligible Alberta R&D expenditure up to the corporation's "base amount"—calculated on Lines 114, 116, and 118 of AT1 Schedule 29 as the average of the corporation's eligible Alberta R&D expenditures over the two immediately preceding taxation years—earns an 8% refundable payment8. Under Tier 2 (Part II calculation), every dollar of current-year eligible Alberta R&D expenditure exceeding that two-year historical base amount (up to the $4,000,000 cap) earns an additional 12% refundable enhancement, producing a combined 20% refundable rate on the incremental growth slice8.

To see how this rolling baseline operates, suppose an Alberta corporation incurred $1,200,000 of eligible Alberta R&D expenditures in Year 1 and $1,800,000 in Year 2, establishing a two-year historical base amount for Year 3 of $1,500,000 (($1,200,000 + $1,800,000) ÷ 2)21. If the corporation spends $3,000,000 in Year 3, the first $1,500,000 (at or below the baseline) earns $120,000 (8% × $1,500,000) and the incremental $1,500,000 above the baseline earns $300,000 (20% × $1,500,000), yielding a total refundable IEG entitlement of $420,00021. If the same corporation spent the full $4,000,000 cap in Year 3, the first $1,500,000 would earn $120,000 and the remaining $2,500,000 would earn $500,000 (20% × $2,500,000), producing a cap-constrained credit of $620,00021. The $4,000,000 maximum expenditure limit is shared among associated corporations and phases out linearly for corporations (and associated groups) with prior-year federal taxable capital employed in Canada (from T2 Schedule 33, Line 690, entered on Line 126 of Form AT29) between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000 according to the formula $4,000,000 × [1 − (taxable capital − $10,000,000) ÷ $40,000,000] on Line 128 of AT1 Schedule 2926.

Crucially, following the federal enactment of Bill C-15, Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration (TRA) updated AT1 Schedule 29 to preserve the exclusion of capital expenditures from the Alberta IEG26. Specifically, while taxation years ending before December 16, 2024 used Line 559 of federal Form T661 (total qualified SR&ED expenditures), for all taxation years ending after December 15, 2024, claimants must populate AT1 Schedule 29 using Line 557 of federal Form T661 (federal current qualified SR&ED expenditures only, excluding restored federal capital expenditures reported on Line 558)20. Furthermore, because the Alberta IEG reduces federal qualified expenditures on federal Line 513, the Alberta TRA Guide to Claiming the Innovation Employment Grant mandates a two-step calculation: Step 1 computes the Alberta IEG on pre-grind federal current qualified expenditures (Line 557 prior to deducting the IEG), and Step 2 deducts the resulting IEG on federal Form T661 Line 513 before computing the federal 35% or 15% ITC, with Alberta disbursing the IEG refund only after the CRA completes its verification of the federal SR&ED claim19.
British Columbia, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Atlantic Provinces, and Yukon

Among the remaining jurisdictions, British Columbia acted as the primary provincial "Follower" after Bill C-15, expressly aligning its 10% BC SR&ED Tax Credit (claimed on T2 Schedule 429) with the federal reforms by extending refundable credit access to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations, restoring capital expenditures as qualifying B.C. expenditures, and widening its prior-year taxable capital phase-out corridor to $15,000,000 to $75,000,0008. Manitoba continues to administer its independent 15% Manitoba R&D Tax Credit under Section 7.3 of the Income Tax Act (Manitoba) (claimed on T2 Schedule 380 within 1 year after the T2 filing due date), where 50% of the credit (7.5%) is refundable for in-house R&D (100% refundable for eligible contract R&D with educational institutions) and the remaining 7.5% is non-refundable (with a 3-year carryback and 20-year carryforward); notably, Manitoba never repealed capital expenditures in 2014 and continues to include depreciable capital property other than buildings and leasehold interests in buildings, while permitting corporations to renounce the credit within 6 months of tax year-end for federal purposes8. Saskatchewan provides a 10% R&D tax credit on T2 Schedule 403 (Line 631 of Schedule 5), which is refundable on the first $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures for CCPCs and non-refundable above $1,000,00061. Finally, Nova Scotia (T2 Schedule 340, Line 566 of Schedule 5, filed within 18 months of year-end), New Brunswick (T2 Schedule 360), Newfoundland and Labrador (T2 Schedule 301), and Yukon (T2 Schedule 442, Line 698 of Schedule 5) each provide a 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit with no expenditure cap, with Yukon offering an additional 5% refundable bonus (20% total) on eligible R&D payments made to Yukon University8.
Worked Federal-Provincial Stacking Calculation (2026 Taxation Year)

To demonstrate the exact statutory mechanics of federal-provincial credit stacking, consider a qualifying CCPC in Ontario (with $5,000,000 in prior-year taxable capital and $200,000 in prior-year taxable income) that incurs $1,000,000 in direct non-specified employee SR&ED salaries in Ontario during its taxation year ended December 31, 2026, elects the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Method on Line 160, and waives the 3.5% non-refundable ORDTC under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario) to maximise immediate cash recovery5.

In the first stage of the calculation, the corporation determines its pre-grind federal qualified expenditure base by combining its $1,000,000 of direct SR&ED salaries (reported on Line 300 and Line 380 of Form T661) with the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount computed in Part 5 under Subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations (55% × $1,000,000 = $550,000), yielding $1,550,000 in pre-assistance qualified expenditures11. In the second stage, because the $1,550,000 expenditure base falls within Ontario's $3,000,000 expenditure limit on T2 Schedule 566, the corporation earns an 8% refundable Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC) equal to $124,000 (8% × $1,550,000)7. In the third stage, because provincial R&D tax credits constitute government assistance under Subsection 127(9) of the federal Income Tax Act, the $124,000 OITC is deducted on Line 513 of federal Form T661, reducing net federal qualified SR&ED expenditures on Line 559 to $1,426,000 ($1,550,000 − $124,000)13. In the fourth stage, the corporation claims the enhanced 35% federal SR&ED Investment Tax Credit on T2 Schedule 31 (well within the new $6,000,000 federal expenditure limit), generating $499,100 (35% × $1,426,000) in 100% refundable federal cash credits2. Summing the $124,000 refundable Ontario OITC and the $499,100 refundable federal ITC produces a total combined cash refund of $623,100—representing an effective cash recovery rate of 62.31% of the corporation's $1,000,000 direct R&D payroll outlay (or 40.20% of the $1,550,000 proxy-loaded expenditure base)11.
Compliance Architecture, Form T661 (Version 26), Pre-Claim Approval, and Audit Defence
The Absolute 18-Month Statutory Filing Deadline (Subsection 37(11))

Under Subsection 37(11) and Paragraph 127(9)(m) of the Income Tax Act, a claimant cannot deduct an expenditure under Section 37 or claim an ITC under Section 127 unless it files the prescribed forms containing the prescribed information on or before its SR&ED reporting deadline—defined as the day that is 12 months after the taxpayer's income tax return filing due date for the taxation year1. Because a corporation's T2 income tax return is due 6 months after the end of its taxation year, the corporate SR&ED reporting deadline falls exactly 18 months after the end of the taxation year; for example, a corporation with a December 31, 2024 taxation year-end faces an absolute statutory filing deadline of June 30, 2026, while a December 31, 2025 year-end faces an absolute deadline of June 30, 20271. For an individual carrying on an unincorporated business (whose T1 return is due June 15 of the following calendar year), the reporting deadline is June 15 of the second following year (17.5 months after the December 31 year-end), whereas for a trust (whose T3 return is due 90 days after year-end), the deadline is 15 months after year-end17.

Crucially, the 18-month reporting deadline in Subsection 37(11) is a strict statutory bar with no administrative mechanism for extension: the Ministerial discretion and taxpayer relief provisions under the Income Tax Act do not apply to extend the SR&ED filing deadline except in narrow statutory reassessment contexts1. If a claimant fails to submit both Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 (or Form T2038(IND) for individuals) containing the prescribed technical project descriptions and line-item expenditure figures before the 18-month deadline expires, the entire SR&ED claim for that taxation year is permanently disallowed by operation of law1. For a partnership, the partnership itself must file a single Form T661 with its T5013 Partnership Information Return reporting 100% of the partnership's SR&ED expenditures (rather than a single partner's share), and individual partners claim their allocated share of the ITC without adding the partnership's SR&ED costs to their own Section 37 pools15.

As Guide T4088 emphasizes, technical narratives must be authored by, or written in the precise technical language and style of, the engineers or scientists who performed the actual work, avoiding marketing hyperbole or vague summaries18. On Line 242, the narrative must distinguish the underlying system-level scientific or technological uncertainty (such as structural trade-offs between algorithmic throughput, latency, memory footprint, or biochemical stability) from the company's commercial product objective3. On Line 244, the claimant must present a chronological, hypothesis-driven account detailing the baseline metrics, the specific hypotheses formulated to reduce or eliminate the uncertainty, the quantitative experiments or analyses executed to test those hypotheses, the empirical results obtained, and how failed iterations informed subsequent hypotheses18. On Line 246, the narrative must articulate the new scientific or technological advancement achieved—or attempted—as a result of the investigation relative to the industry baseline prior to the tax year3. Notably, regarding Lines 270 to 282 (the supporting evidence checklist in Section C of Part 2), Guide T4088 confirms that while claimants do not submit supporting documents with the initial tax return, they must retain them for review; moreover, if a claimant inadvertently fails to tick an evidence box when initially filing Form T661, the claimant is still legally permitted to submit that contemporaneous evidence to the CRA reviewer during an audit even after the 18-month reporting deadline has passed17.
The April 1, 2026 Pre-Claim Approval Process and CRA Audit Defence Protocols

In the most recent reporting year, the CRA accepted 90% of filed SR&ED claims as filed, accepted a further 6% after modifications, and denied only 4% in their entirety—meaning roughly 96% of filed claims resulted in allowed tax credits2. However, when a claim is selected for technical and financial review (which occurs for approximately 20% to 25% of filings, with heightened selection probability for first-time claimants and large refund claims), the standard CRA service target is 180 calendar days from receipt of a complete claim1.

To provide earlier certainty and accelerate working capital inflows, the CRA launched the elective Pre-Claim Approval Process on April 1, 20262. Under this mechanism, an eligible corporation may submit its planned or ongoing R&D projects to the CRA prior to filing its tax return to obtain an upfront technical determination on whether the work satisfies the scientific and technological eligibility criteria of Subsection 248(1)14. The CRA aims to issue a formal eligibility determination within eight weeks of receiving a pre-claim application14. Where a claimant secures Pre-Claim Approval and its subsequent T661 filing is selected for an expenditure verification review, the CRA's processing service standard is cut in half—from 180 calendar days to 90 calendar days1.

During a formal CRA review, the claim is evaluated by two distinct specialists: a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) (a domain specialist with an academic or industrial background in software, engineering, chemistry, or life sciences who assesses Part 2 technical eligibility under Northwest Hydraulic) and a Financial Reviewer (an accounting auditor who verifies Part 3, Part 4, and Part 5 expenditure calculations, T4 reconciliations, time tracking, contract agreements, and Subsection 78(4) payment proof)1.

To withstand dual RTA and Financial Reviewer scrutiny under the post-Bill C-15 statutory regime, corporate claimants must embed five audit-ready governance practices into their ongoing R&D operations1. First, enterprises should implement automated contemporaneous evidence capture by integrating SR&ED tagging directly into daily engineering workflows—linking Git commit histories, Jira or Linear tickets, CI/CD build failure logs, laboratory notebooks, and quantitative benchmark runs (such as latency logs or pH and microbial assays as validated in Manning Canning Kitchens, 2024 TCC 159) directly to specific dated hypotheses before and during the experimental work1. Second, claimants must maintain granular bi-weekly or monthly time-tracking records tying each employee's hours to specific SR&ED projects versus routine commercial engineering, and where a founder or specified employee is claimed at 90% or more (all or substantially all), retain calendar logs, organizational charts, and operational records proving which other personnel handled non-SR&ED corporate administration and sales1. Third, corporate legal and finance teams must maintain strict cap table and corporate association hygiene, keeping a dated share register of every share issuance, option exercise, and financing round to identify the exact dates any employee crossed or fell below the 10% specified shareholder threshold, while verifying all associated corporations globally to ensure timely filing of the $6,000,000 federal expenditure limit allocation on T2 Schedule 49 and compliance with the $186,500 specified employee proxy cap under ITR Subsection 2900(8)4. Fourth, for every piece of depreciable equipment or GPU compute cluster acquired after December 15, 2024, claimants must institute machine-utilisation logging that records total operating hours versus SR&ED project operating hours to substantiate the 90% ASA threshold on Line 390 or the 50% to 90% Shared-Use Equipment threshold on Line 504, and accurately report the 10 most expensive depreciable properties and their project operating time percentages on Line 263 of Version 26 of Form T6611. Finally, corporate controllers should execute a mandatory 150-day accrual clearance audit five months after the corporate tax year-end to ensure that all accrued SR&ED wages, subcontractor invoices, and material payables are settled in cash prior to Day 180, thereby preventing involuntary statutory disallowances under Subsection 78(4) and Line 528 of Form T6615.
